claims.text: Cryo-rolling followed by annealing is the proposed intervention.
Cryo-rolling and annealing can overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
Cryo-rolling and annealing can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
The starting alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The applicable testing and operating condition is room temperature.
The intervention produces fine lamellar regions containing FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains and B2 lamellae.
The intervention produces coarse non-lamellar regions containing ultrafine FCC grains, a few coarse recrystallized FCC grains, and relatively coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase.
The resulting hierarchical microstructure leads to improved mechanical properties.
The treated alloy will have a yield strength greater than 1400 MPa.
The treated alloy will have an ultimate tensile strength greater than 1500 MPa.
The treated alloy will have elongation to failure greater than 10%.
Strength and ductility will both be enhanced relative to the as-cast material.
The as-cast material has an excellent combination of strength and ductility at room temperature.
The exact mechanism of cryo-rolling and annealing is not fully understood.
More specific evidence is needed to establish the relationship between the hierarchical microstructure and enhanced mechanical properties.
Validation requires at least a 10% increase in yield strength and a 5% increase in elongation to failure relative to the as-cast control.

contradictions.description: The initial state and structural mediator are both described as the same hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, while the mechanism says the intervention creates the hierarchical microstructure. This obscures what structural change actually mediates the improvement.

The hypothesis characterizes the starting material as having limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness, whereas the baseline calls the as-cast material an excellent strength-ductility combination.
